item.title: The COP31 climate talks in Antalya ended on Sunday without a final agreement after more than two weeks, the first major failure to reach agreement at UN climate talks since Copenhagen in 2009, Business Day reports.
item.description:
The UN climate conference COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, collapsed on Sunday with no final agreement after more than two weeks of negotiations, Business Day reports, the first major failure to reach agreement at UN climate talks since the Copenhagen summit in 2009; almost 200 parties failed to agree. Earlier, a draft presented by Australia and Türkiye was rejected by the EU and its member states because it did not mention fossil fuels, and Germany's environment minister Carsten Schneider called it "not eligible for approval", Handelsblatt reports. A previous draft decision text, released on Thursday, had dropped calls to phase out fossil fuels and set the summit on track to endorse proposals to increase electrification; organisers sought support for a voluntary pledge to raise electricity's share of global final energy demand to 35% by 2035, from just over 20% now, LiveMint reports. The Confederation of Finnish Industries (EK) called the outcome a disappointment for business because it made no progress on reducing fossil fuel use, while noting the rise of electrification on the international climate agenda. The European Steel Association Eurofer said during the talks, as world leaders gathered for COP31, that climate ambition and the cost industries pay for emissions remain highly divergent worldwide. The rows do not say whether any decisions or voluntary pledges were adopted separately.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The talks ended without an agreed text, and the EU had rejected the last reported draft because it did not mention fossil fuels. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, without an agreed text the direction of climate policy in the coming year is set by national and regional measures rather than by a global decision, which keeps differences in carbon costs between regions in place, which matters for energy-intensive industries such as chemicals that compete across regions with different carbon prices. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, European producers continue to carry carbon costs that competitors in some other regions do not, and customer demand for lower-carbon products will depend more on regional rules and company targets than on a global commitment. Points that may be worth considering include whether a voluntary electrification pledge is pursued outside the formal text, EU positions ahead of the next conference, and changes to carbon border measures between trading partners.

Business Day | Handelsblatt | LiveMint | EK | Eurofer

item.title: A WHO and UN Environment Programme report calls endocrine-disrupting chemicals a "global and growing threat", with health and environmental costs conservatively estimated at over USD 1 trillion a year.
item.description:
The "State of the Science of Endocrine-Disrupting Chemicals 2026" report by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) was released at the First International Conference of the Global Framework on Chemicals, according to IPEN. The report finds evidence of health concerns from endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) in all regions of the world and says its findings suggest that endocrine disruption contributes to a significant share of the global burden of non-communicable disease. EDCs are found across many chemical groups, including many plastic chemicals; IPEN names bisphenols and phthalates, used in plastics for decades, which the report associates with increasing risks of conditions including infertility and several cancers. Japan Today reports that the report calls EDCs a "global and growing threat" and conservatively estimates the health and environmental costs of exposure at over USD 1 trillion a year. EDCs are found in products from toys and make-up to building materials and clothing, and workers in the chemicals and recycling industries, particularly in countries with weak regulation, are among those most at risk. The report also notes that many pesticides are EDCs. The rows do not give the report's regulatory recommendations for plastics chemicals or any government response.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The report is a scientific assessment by two UN bodies, not a regulation, and it was released at the first conference of the Global Framework on Chemicals. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, assessments of this kind tend to feed into national and regional chemical regulation over several years, and a cost estimate of over USD 1 trillion a year gives regulators a figure to weigh against the cost of substitution. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, some adhesive and sealant formulations use bisphenol-based resins or phthalate plasticisers, so further restrictions on these substance groups would add reformulation and testing work, with building and consumer applications likely to be examined first. Points that may be worth considering include regulatory responses in the EU and other regions, follow-up under the Global Framework on Chemicals, and customer requests for EDC-free formulations.

IPEN | Japan Today

item.title: Spain's government plans to extend its bank levy into 2027, expected to raise EUR 1.4 billion for social housing construction, tenant tax incentives and home renovation, with a cabinet decision due on 24 November, before the 29 November election.
item.description:
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced on 21 November that the government would approve an extension of the current banking levy to 2027 to fund housing policies, The Straits Times reports. The tax is expected to raise EUR 1.4 billion, and the revenue is to go in full to the construction of social housing, tax incentives for tenants and the renovation of homes. Handelsblatt reports that the cabinet is to decide on the levy on 24 November, shortly before the parliamentary election on 29 November. Spain first introduced the extraordinary tax in 2022 for two years and extended it at the end of 2024 for another three years; in its current form it taxes commissions and fees at a progressive rate of up to 7% for institutions with revenues above EUR 5 billion, and applies to profits for 2024 to 2026. Sánchez called the snap election in October to harness the momentum from mass housing protests, The Straits Times reports. The rows do not give how the EUR 1.4 billion is split between the three uses or when it would be spent.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The measure is a funding plan announced shortly before the 29 November election, with the cabinet due to decide on it on 24 November. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, revenue earmarked for social housing construction and renovation adds public demand to a construction market in which housing has become a central political issue. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, social housing construction and home renovation use tile adhesives, sealants, flooring and insulation materials, and renovation spending tends to reach these products sooner than new building. Points that may be worth considering include the cabinet decision on 24 November, the outcome of the 29 November election, and how the funds are divided between new building and renovation.

The Straits Times | Handelsblatt

item.title: Six Japanese carmakers — Toyota, Honda, Isuzu, Mitsubishi, Mazda and Nissan — will together invest more than THB 134 billion in Thailand in 2026–2030 to upgrade production for electrified and biofuel vehicles and local components.
item.description:
Toyota, Honda, Isuzu, Mitsubishi, Mazda and Nissan will collectively invest more than THB 134 billion in Thailand between 2026 and 2030, The Nation reports. The investment is to upgrade production bases for new models and technologies, with a focus on producing electrified vehicles of various types, biofuel-powered cars and key components locally. Toyota plans to build hydrogen fuel cell pick-ups in Thailand for export, and Mazda aims to set up production lines for mild hybrids. The report also describes Thailand's new vehicle tax structure, which is designed to encourage long-term investment, develop Thailand as a base for producing and exporting environmentally friendly vehicles and raise the value of locally made parts. From 1 January 2027, fully built imported battery-electric and range-extended electric vehicles will face a 35% excise duty where there is no production base in Thailand; for imports by brands with a Thai base and for vehicles made in Thailand, tax treatment will be linked to investment, employment and the use of local parts. The row does not give a split by company or year, capacity figures, or whether the amounts include investments announced earlier. It comes from one source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The plans cover six Japanese carmakers together, and Thailand's new tax structure links tax treatment to investment, employment and the use of local parts. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, linking vehicle taxes to local content tends to move component and material sourcing closer to the assembly plants, and a shift to electrified vehicles changes which components are made locally. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, local production of electrified vehicles and their components increases the use of bonding, sealing and thermal-management materials in Thailand, and local-content rules can favour suppliers that produce in the country. Points that may be worth considering include company-level investment and timing, how the local-parts criteria are defined, and Thai vehicle production and export data in 2027.

The Nation

item.title: The US Senate voted 62–33 to pass a bipartisan bill that aims to shorten permitting timelines for energy and infrastructure projects, with new limits on lawsuits and on the scope and length of environmental reviews.
item.description:
The US Senate voted 62–33 on Thursday to pass a bipartisan bill that aims to reduce permitting timelines for energy and infrastructure projects, Axios reports. The bill sets new limits on the duration of lawsuits and on the scope and length of reviews under the Clean Water Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, and includes language that would make it more difficult to revoke permits once issued, which Axios describes as a priority for renewables groups and for Democrats unhappy with barriers set by the Trump administration. It also includes provisions to ensure that data centres pay for needed grid upgrades and expands federal authority over the siting and approval of certain interstate transmission projects. The Association of Equipment Manufacturers (AEM) names the legislation the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 and says a more predictable permitting process lets projects move from planning to construction faster. The rows do not say what the next legislative step is or when the bill could take effect.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The bill addresses permitting timelines, litigation and review limits, and AEM says a more predictable process would let projects move from planning to construction faster and unlock investment. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, shorter review and litigation periods can bring forward construction of power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure, provided the bill passes the remaining legislative steps. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, earlier project starts would bring forward demand for construction materials, including sealants, coatings and bonding products used in energy and infrastructure construction and in data-centre buildings. Points that may be worth considering include the bill's next legislative steps, the final text on review limits, and how the data-centre grid provisions are applied.

Axios | AEM

item.title: The EU and UK announced deals at their 20 November summit to link their carbon markets and cut agri-food checks, with implementation not yet formalised, and no delay was announced to stricter electric-car rules of origin due on 1 January 2027.
item.description:
At their summit in Brussels on 20 November, the UK and the EU agreed to remove trade barriers, link their carbon markets and scrap some food checks, The Straits Times reports. Il Sole 24 Ore reports that the package provides for the elimination of certifications and controls for cross-border trade in animals, plants and food products, which the UK government estimates could bring economic benefits of up to GBP 5.1 billion a year, and that the agreement on emissions markets would avoid the reciprocal application of carbon tariffs to products such as steel. Up to 100,000 young adults from each side are to be allowed to live and work in the other for up to three years, The Straits Times reports. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the deal would add up to GBP 17 billion a year to the UK economy, MarketScreener reports. Il Sole 24 Ore reports that implementation has yet to be formalised; according to Handelsblatt, the EU's view is that implementation follows only after an outstanding agreement on tuition fees, which the two sides aim to reach within six months according to The Straits Times, while London speaks of a "done deal". Opening the EU's "Made in Europe" initiative to UK companies is still under negotiation, Handelsblatt reports. The summit ended without an announced postponement of stricter rules of origin for electric cars and their batteries from 1 January 2027, Yahoo reports, so cars that do not meet them risk losing duty-free access. Carmakers' associations ACEA and SMMT have asked for a solution to keep electric car exports to the UK from facing 10% duties from January, with 80% of those exports at risk, Les Echos reports. As the summit got under way, Cefic and the Chemical Industries Association (CIA) said the EU and UK were each other's largest chemical export markets by volume in 2025. The rows do not give the timetable for linking the carbon markets or the products covered.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Two parts of the summit bear directly on industrial trade: the carbon-market link, which the reporting says would avoid mutual carbon tariffs on products such as steel, and the electric-car rules of origin, for which no postponement was announced. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, linked carbon markets bring carbon costs for covered goods closer together on both sides, which reduces the need for border charges between them, while an EU interpretation that ties implementation to a separate agreement on fees means the timing is not settled. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, closely integrated chemical supply chains across the Channel benefit from fewer differences in carbon costs and rules, and a 10% duty on EU electric-car exports to the UK from January would weigh on vehicle production volumes in plants that export there, and with them on demand for bonding and sealing materials in vehicle and battery assembly. Points that may be worth considering include the formal texts and their timetable, whether a solution on electric-car rules of origin is found before 1 January, and whether UK companies are included in "Made in Europe".

The Straits Times | Il Sole 24 Ore | Handelsblatt | Handelsblatt | MarketScreener | Yahoo | Les Echos | Cefic

item.title: US apartment construction starts totalled about 76,000 units in the third quarter, the lowest quarterly total since 2012, and units under construction declined for a 14th consecutive quarter to about 593,000, Apartments.com data show.
item.description:
Apartment construction starts in the US totalled about 76,000 units in the third quarter of 2026, 63% below the peak of nearly 206,000 units in the first quarter of 2022 and the lowest quarterly total since 2012, according to Apartments.com's multifamily construction update, published by MarketScreener. Over the past 12 months, starts totalled about 342,000 units, the lowest annual pace since 2014 and roughly three-quarters of the units delivered over the same period. About 593,000 units were under construction nationwide in the third quarter, roughly half the early-2023 peak of nearly 1.2 million and the 14th consecutive quarterly decline, which returns the pipeline to mid-2016 levels. About 446,000 units were delivered over the past four quarters, 22% fewer than a year earlier and 36% below the 2024 peak. New York City has the largest pipeline, with about 46,000 units, followed by Dallas-Fort Worth with about 32,000. The row does not give the change from the second quarter, reasons for the decline or figures for single-family housing.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Starts below deliveries mean the number of apartments under construction keeps shrinking, and completions are already falling. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, apartments started now are finished over the following one to two years, so a starts level at its lowest since 2012 points to fewer apartment completions through 2027 and into 2028. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, multifamily construction uses flooring adhesives, sealants, waterproofing and insulation materials mostly in the later building phases, so the effect of low starts reaches these products with a delay, while renovation of existing stock is not covered by these figures. Points that may be worth considering include whether starts stabilise in the fourth quarter, the pace of decline in completions, and differences between regional pipelines.

MarketScreener

item.title: IG Metall called full-day warning strikes at metal and electrical industry companies in nearly all of Germany on 20 November, including at BMW and Audi, and a strike of more than 23,000 employees at 19 northern companies for 23 November.
item.description:
IG Metall called on thousands of workers in the metal and electrical industry to hold full-day warning strikes in nearly all of Germany on Friday, 20 November, including at BMW and Audi, Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports. In Bavaria, tens of thousands of employees at 18 companies took part, some in strikes lasting 24 hours, with large sites of BMW, Audi and Bosch among those affected, according to Süddeutsche Zeitung, which reports that further warning strikes were announced for the following week. Commercial Times reports that the union called a strike for 23 November involving more than 23,000 employees from 19 companies in northern Germany, including Mercedes-Benz, the Meyer Werft shipyard and Siemens Gamesa. The union demands 5% more pay and job security for 3.7 million employees. Employers offer a one-time payment and a permanent increase of 1.3% from July 2028, FAZ reports, with no increase for the first 20 months, according to Commercial Times. The two sides also disagree on deviations from collectively agreed standards: IG Metall makes concessions conditional on binding investment and job commitments, while employers want automatic options to deviate. The rows do not give production losses, the total number of strikers nationwide or a date for the next negotiating round.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The dispute covers the metal and electrical industry; in Bavaria the reported strikes focused on the automotive industry, with large sites of BMW, Audi and Bosch affected, while the northern strike also includes Meyer Werft and Siemens Gamesa. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, full-day strikes interrupt production at the plants concerned for a day or more, and repeated rounds can delay deliveries along supply chains; the outcome on pay and on deviations from collective standards bears on labour costs and location decisions in German manufacturing beyond this round. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, short stoppages at carmakers and suppliers mainly shift orders for bonding and sealing materials in time rather than remove them, while a settlement that raises labour costs, or one that ties pay to investment commitments, can affect how much production stays in Germany. Points that may be worth considering include the date of the next negotiating round, whether strikes spread to more plants, and how the question of deviations from collective standards is settled.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Commercial Times | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: Euroconstruct now expects construction volume in its 19 European countries to grow 1.2% in real terms in 2026, down from the 2.0% it forecast in June, with output in Germany, France, Italy and Austria still below 2023 levels in 2029.
item.description:
Euroconstruct, a network of research institutes from 19 European countries that publishes forecasts for the European construction industry twice a year, expects the construction volume of the 19 countries to rise 1.2% in real terms in 2026, according to a report published by Wallstreet:online. In June the institutes had expected an increase of 2.0%. They expect the recovery to gain momentum from 2027, but construction output in Austria, France, Italy and Germany is expected to remain below its 2023 level even in 2029. Austria's real construction volume is expected to be 5.8% below its 2023 level in 2029, the largest gap among the 19 countries. The row does not give a split by segment (residential, non-residential, civil engineering), the growth rate expected for 2027, separate figures for Germany, France or Italy, or the reasons for the lower 2026 estimate.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The revision concerns a year that is close to its end, and the four countries named as staying below 2023 levels include Germany, France and Italy. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a forecast cut this late in the year largely reflects activity already observed, so it points to weaker European construction in 2026 than expected in June, and output that is still below 2023 levels in 2029 in several large markets points to a long period of low volumes rather than a quick rebound. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, construction volume drives demand for tile adhesives, sealants, flooring and insulation materials, and a recovery concentrated in some countries while large markets lag would shift demand between national markets rather than lift it evenly. Points that may be worth considering include the segment and country detail of the full Euroconstruct forecast, how the expected recovery from 2027 divides between new building and renovation, and German permit and order data in the coming months.

Wallstreet:online

item.title: Brent crude was down 0.7% at USD 91.36 a barrel at 11:20 GMT on 20 November and on track for a third straight weekly fall, as crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels.
item.description:
Oil prices, which edged higher early on 20 November according to Business Recorder, were lower by 11:20 GMT and set for a third consecutive weekly decline, Yahoo Finance reports: Brent crude futures were down 0.7%, or USD 0.62, at USD 91.36 a barrel at 11:20 GMT, and US West Texas Intermediate for December delivery was down 1% at USD 82.40. According to the report, expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels, despite Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the strait. The two reports give different weekly figures: Yahoo Finance says Brent was on track for a 5% weekly decline, while an earlier report the same day, carried by Business Recorder, gives 3.5%, so no single weekly figure is stated here. On 23 November oil fell again as a selloff in wider financial markets, linked to concerns about the ability of the AI sector to boost economic growth, spilled over into commodities, while continuing attacks on Gulf shipping limited the losses, MarketScreener reports; that report gives no price level. The rows do not give refined-product or naphtha prices, or the volumes now passing through the strait.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The reported driver of the weekly declines to 20 November is restored supply through the strait, while the further fall on 23 November is attributed to a wider financial-market selloff, and attacks on shipping in the region continued in the same period. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a price that falls for several weeks while attacks continue suggests the market is weighting restored flows more heavily than the risk of new disruption, which leaves room for renewed price swings if flows are interrupted again. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, crude prices reach petrochemical feedstocks, resins and solvents with a lag, and how much of a crude decline reaches raw-material costs depends on whether refined-product and naphtha prices follow. Points that may be worth considering include whether the weekly declines continue, refined-product price moves, and the cost of shipping and insurance in the Gulf.

Yahoo | Business Recorder | MarketScreener
